name: Cockburn Street
description: The curve of the street pulls your eye upward: sandstone tenements rising in a gentle S-bend down toward Waverley, carved here and there with a small monogram, 'PK', if you know where to spot it. You're walking on a street that didn't exist until 1856, when engineers sliced a whole new shortcut straight through a knot of medieval closes to link the Royal Mile with the railway station below. It's named for Henry, Lord Cockburn, a judge celebrated for campaigning to protect Edinburgh's old buildings — a little ironic, since building his namesake street meant bulldozing straight through several of them. These days the serpentine curve is known for something Lord Cockburn probably never predicted: a run of independent, alternative and gothic-leaning boutiques that made Cockburn Street Edinburgh's unofficial home of subculture shopping.

name: Craig's Close
description: Squeeze into Craig's Close and the walls close in fast: this is the narrowest of the surviving original lanes off the Royal Mile, tight enough in places to touch both sides at once. In the 1700s, a tavern here called the Isle of Man Arms hosted the Cape Club, a drinking society whose members took mock-chivalric titles — 'Sir Precenter', 'Sir Forgetful' — and were inducted with a raised fire-poker over a solemn oath, every meeting wound up strictly before 1am, no gambling allowed. The poet Robert Fergusson drank here as 'Sir Precenter'; so did a far less respectable member, Deacon William Brodie, Edinburgh's own double life split between respectable cabinetmaker and city councillor by day and burglar by night, a real case that helped inspire Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

name: Old Fishmarket Close
description: Walk into Old Fishmarket Close and you're following a slope fish once tumbled down for three centuries: the close took its name from the market that operated here, first recorded in council minutes in 1539. Stand still and picture 1573, when government cannon battered the High Street during the 'Lang Siege' — the story goes that fish were sent flying clean out of the market stalls onto the surrounding rooftops, with hungry townsfolk scrambling up after them. A grimmer record: in April 1585, a girl working in this close became the first person in Edinburgh recorded to die when plague reached the city. And in 1705, in one of the close's flats, a Dutchman named Abraham Sever kept a pet elephant, nicknamed the 'Dundee Elephant', as a lodger in a medieval Edinburgh tenement.

name: Anchor Close
description: Duck into Anchor Close and you're standing where the modern reference book was born: a small print shop here, run by William Smellie, produced the first-ever edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica in the 1770s. Smellie also printed the first Edinburgh edition of Robert Burns's poems in 1787, and Burns himself spent hours in this close correcting the proofs. The two men's friendship ran to less scholarly pursuits too: Smellie founded a drinking club, the Crochallan Fencibles, which met at the Anchor Tavern here under landlady Fanny Douglas, and it was for this club's private amusement that Burns wrote his most explicit collection of verse, The Merry Muses of Caledonia, kept unpublished and passed around in manuscript for decades because it was considered far too indecent for print.

name: Tron Kirk Market
description: The clock on the Tron's stone steeple is the timepiece that, for generations, the whole city set its New Year by. Crowds used to pack the High Street outside to hear the Tron's bells ring in Hogmanay at midnight, long before Princes Street Gardens took over as the official party. The church itself was built in the 1630s and 40s, and takes its name from the 'tron', the public weighing beam that once stood outside it, used to check traders weren't short-changing customers in the market that gathered here. It survived as a working parish church until 1952, when a shrinking, depopulated Old Town could no longer support a congregation, and it sat empty for decades before an unlikely second life: today, restored, it houses a market of independent designers and makers, trading resuming, just without the beam.

name: The Milkman
description: The shopfront still has timber shutters that still slide down into slots below the window, an original feature from when this was a confectioner's shop, part of a row built in 1859 to unify Cockburn Street's newly cut frontage. The hand-painted lettering on the fascia dates back just as far, carefully restored rather than replaced when the current coffee shop moved in. The Milkman opened here in 2015, its name borrowed from the founder's great-grandfather, the last horse-drawn milkman working in the small Aberdeenshire town of Huntly, a nod to a much older, slower way of delivering something good to your door, now reworked as flat whites instead of milk bottles.

name: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box
description: That ordinary-looking pillar box on the corner isn't red because it was never meant to blend in: it's gold, and it's stayed that way since the summer of 2012. Royal Mail repainted a postbox gold in the hometown of every British athlete who won an Olympic gold medal at London 2012, and Edinburgh's track cyclist Sir Chris Hoy won two, so the city got two gold boxes. This one, in Hunter Square, marks his win in the men's Keirin. Look closely and you'll still find the sprint medal's twin marker across town at Hanover Street and Princes Street, a quiet piece of 2012 nostalgia hiding in plain sight on an otherwise unremarkable street corner.

name: Old Saint Paul's Scottish Episcopal Church
description: Head down the steep steps off Jeffrey Street and you drop straight into a hidden nave, tucked below street level, lit by dim stained glass rather than daylight. The congregation here traces itself back to 1689, when the last bishop of St Giles', Alexander Rose, refused to accept Presbyterian church government and led his followers out to worship instead in a converted wool store down nearby Carrubber's Close. From there, this Episcopalian congregation became entangled in Scotland's most dangerous politics: many members backed the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745, and paid for it, harassed and persecuted under law for decades, only shaking off their reputation for treason after the death of Bonnie Prince Charlie himself in 1788. The current building, finished in 1883, has since been extended twice, its length now three times the original.

name: Margaret Tait Filmmaker Plaque
description: Pause here for a name easy to miss among North Bridge's grander landmarks: Margaret Tait, one of Scotland's most singular filmmakers, commemorated for a career the mainstream mostly ignored while she was alive to see it. Tait trained first as a doctor, served in the Royal Army Medical Corps during the Second World War, then went to Rome to study filmmaking before returning to Scotland to make what she called 'film poems', short, intensely observed studies of ordinary life and place, largely self-funded because the British film establishment showed little interest. She didn't direct her first and only feature film, Blue Black Permanent, until 1992, at the age of 74, making her the first Scottish woman to direct a feature-length film, recognition that arrived only after decades spent almost entirely outside the industry she quietly outlasted.

name: The Scotsman Picturehouse
description: Inside the Scotsman Hotel, tucked into what used to be a disused room, are red leather armchairs, individual table lamps and Edwardian cornicing wrapped around one of Edinburgh's smallest cinemas. The building above you is the real story: a 190-foot tower raised in the early 1900s as the grand headquarters of The Scotsman newspaper, marking a triumphant new entrance to the Old Town after North Bridge itself was rebuilt in 1897 - its own construction history, including a genuine disaster, is told at the North Bridge stop on this route. The Scotsman printed the news from this tower for ninety years, until the paper moved out in 1999 and the building was reborn, first as a hotel, then as this boutique picture house.

name: O'Neill's Bar
description: Notice how orderly Hunter Square feels compared to the tangle of closes just off it: that's because, unlike almost everything around it, this square wasn't grown over centuries, but planned. It was laid out in the 1780s as part of the hugely controversial South Bridge Improvement Scheme, a project so fiercely opposed it was delayed for a decade before finally demolishing entire wynds of housing and workshops to make way for South Bridge and the streets around it, many of the displaced residents were tenants who received no compensation at all for losing their homes. This particular building on the square has swapped identities more recently too: for years it traded as the Tron Bar before a 2025 renovation turned it into this Irish-themed O'Neill's, its Georgian facade kept largely intact even as everything behind it was stripped out and refitted.

name: The Inn on the Mile
description: Giant Doric columns hold up this building's portico - a bank dressed as a temple, a favourite architectural trick of the early 20th century, meant to tell customers their money was safe with people who took themselves very seriously indeed. Built in 1923 as a branch of the British Linen Bank, one of Scotland's oldest banking houses, chartered in 1746 originally to finance the country's linen trade, the building later passed to the Bank of Scotland after a 1970s takeover, before finally being stripped of ledgers and counters altogether and reborn as a boutique hotel and pub. High ceilings, cornicing and the sheer scale of the rooms all still whisper 'bank' underneath the beer taps.

name: Landy's Fish and Chips
description: The width of the room around you gives away a building shaped by disaster: this stretch of North Bridge only exists because of a full rebuild in 1897, after the original 1763 bridge suffered a dramatic construction accident - the full story is told at the North Bridge stop on this route. The chippy itself is a much newer arrival: opened in late 2024 by the Vittoria Group, an Edinburgh-Italian restaurant family that's been frying in Leith since 1970, it's now run by the third generation, serving classic seaside fish and chips in a two-floor, nautical-themed space a world away from the tenements and workshops that once crowded this exact spot.

name: Radisson Blu Hotel
address: The Royal Mile, 80 High St, Edinburgh EH1 1TH, UK
description: Notice how this building manages to look old without actually being old: no fake weathering, no pastiche shopfronts, just traditional Scottish materials and proportions wrapped around a thoroughly modern hotel. It opened in 1990, designed by Scottish architect Ian Begg specifically to fill what was, for years, a conspicuous gap site on the Royal Mile's historic frontage. Begg's solution was a quiet architectural statement: rather than building something overtly modern or trying to fake a genuine historic tenement, he built new in an unashamedly 'Scottish vernacular' style, turrets, small windows, thick stone walls, betting that Edinburgh's Old Town character comes from a way of building, not simply from age. Whatever you make of the result, it's one of very few 20th-century buildings on the Mile trying to speak the same architectural language as its centuries-older neighbours.

name: Carrubber's Close
description: Carrubber's Close is a passage documented since before 1513, one of the oldest lanes on the Mile. After Presbyterians took control of the Church of Scotland in 1690, Episcopalians here had nowhere legal left to worship, so they met in secret in a small chapel down this close, using a wooden altar built to fold flat and vanish if the authorities came looking. Among the students who worshipped here in secret during the 1750s was an American, Samuel Seabury, who later became the first bishop of the Episcopal Church in the United States, a direct line from a hidden altar in an Edinburgh close to the founding of an American religious institution. By the 1880s the close's character had shifted from concealment to conversion: evangelist Dwight L. Moody helped raise the funds to build the Carrubbers Close Mission, whose building still stands here today.

name: North Bridge Arcade
address: 7 North Bridge, Arcade, Edinburgh EH1 1QL, UK
description: Through this doorway, the Royal Mile's noise drops away almost instantly: you're inside a covered Victorian shopping arcade, one of only five left standing in the whole of Scotland. Built in 1900, it still has its original bowed shopfront windows, coffered ceiling and a stained-glass dome overhead, all designed to let daylight flood a passage that otherwise runs, tunnel-like, between North Bridge and Cockburn Street. It opened in the same building boom that gave Edinburgh its rebuilt North Bridge in 1897 - a bridge with its own dramatic backstory, told at the North Bridge stop on this route.

name: Bishop's Close
address: 129 High St, Bishop's Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1SG, UK
description: Bishop's Close marks where, in 1742, one of the most consequential, and controversial, Scots of the 18th century was born: Henry Dundas, later Viscount Melville, whose statue still towers over St Andrew Square. Dundas rose to become one of the most powerful men in the British government, effectively running Scotland's political patronage for decades. But he's remembered today mostly for something else: as Home Secretary in 1792, he proposed a 'gradual' rather than immediate abolition of the slave trade, a delay historians still argue over — critics say it held up abolition until 1807, prolonging the trade's toll by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans; defenders say abolition would have stalled regardless. The debate is very much alive: Edinburgh City Council added a plaque addressing his slavery links to his statue as recently as 2021.

name: The Mitre Bar
description: The name above the door is a clue to something buried underneath your feet: in 1615, this spot was home to a grand tenement belonging to John Spottiswood, then Bishop of St Andrews, and the pub's mitre, a bishop's ceremonial headdress, nods directly to him. That original building burned down in 1814, and the tavern that replaced it kept the bishop's memory alive in name only, or so the story goes: locals still claim his throne lies buried somewhere beneath the current bar, and that his ghost hasn't quite left the building either. Whether or not you believe the haunting, the Mitre's dim lighting, packed bookshelves and old prints of the city make it easy to imagine a 17th-century bishop feeling right at home.

name: Bailie Fyfe's Close
description: The mouth of Bailie Fyfe's Close, looking east along the High Street, sits at the western edge of one of Edinburgh's deadliest nights. On 24 November 1861, an ancient seven-storey tenement between here and neighbouring Paisley Close suddenly gave way in the night, its decayed timbers unable to bear the weight of up to a hundred residents; 35 people died in the rubble. As rescuers worked through the wreckage, a boy's voice rang out from beneath the debris: 'Heave awa', lads, I'm no' deid yet!' He survived, and his defiant cry was carved into the replacement building next door at Paisley Close, above a sculpted likeness of his face, that close now nicknamed the 'Heave Awa' Hoose'. The close itself is named after Gilbert Fyfe, a merchant and city 'bailie' who lived here in the 1680s; later residents included the young Francis Jeffrey, future founder of the Edinburgh Review.

name: The Nutcracker Christmas Shop
description: Push open the door and you're hit immediately by pine and spice: this small, family-run shop keeps Christmas running all year on a street that has, in various forms, sold goods to passing trade for hundreds of years. Inside, hand-carved German nutcrackers stand shoulder to shoulder with baubles and room fragrances sourced from around the world, continuing a long Royal Mile tradition of tightly packed specialist shops squeezed into narrow tenement frontages, each one making the most of just a few feet of street-level space. It's a reminder that behind the grand history of closes and clubs and kirks that line this street, ordinary retail, someone trying to sell you something useful, or at least sparkly, has been happening here for just as long.

name: Netherbow Wellhead
description: Brass markers are set into the pavement around this monument: they trace the exact footprint of the Netherbow Port, the great fortified gateway that once stood here and formed the true edge of medieval Edinburgh. Anyone passing through it had to pay a toll, even residents, and the poor who couldn't afford it were effectively trapped on one side or the other, which is how this spot earned its enduring nickname, 'World's End': to those who could never afford to leave, the gate really did mark where their known world stopped. The gate itself, rebuilt in 1571, was demolished in 1764 as the city outgrew its walls, but the wellhead beside it survived: designed by Sir William Bruce and built around 1685 by master mason Robert Mylne, it once fed drinking water piped in from burns south of the town to six wells along the High Street.

name: The Albanach
description: The name above the door is the giveaway: 'Albanach' is simply Gaelic for 'Scotsman' or 'Scottish person', a bold, no-nonsense title for a pub sitting on the Royal Mile a short walk from the old Netherbow gate, historically the boundary where medieval Edinburgh itself ended. Inside, the pub backs onto the top of Fleshmarket Close, and its rear windows look straight down that steep lane toward Market Street below, a genuine slice of Old Town topography you can take in with a pint in hand. True to its name, the bar stocks over 220 Scottish malt whiskies, making the case for its Gaelic title one dram at a time.

name: The Advocate
description: You're standing in Hunter Square, a rare piece of planned geometry dropped into Edinburgh's tangled Old Town, laid out in the 1780s as part of the fiercely contested South Bridge Improvement Scheme, a project so unpopular it was delayed a decade before finally flattening entire wynds of housing to build South Bridge and the streets around it. This particular pub has worn several names over the years, most memorably 'Fiscal & Firkin' before rebranding as the Advocate, a nod to the square's proximity to the courts and to St Giles' Cathedral just around the corner, where the city's lawyers still put in a full day's work before some of them wander over here for an evening pint.

name: Malt Shovel Inn
description: Head down to the foot of Cockburn Street and you're standing in a pub that predates the street around it: the Malt Shovel was already trading here in 1800, more than half a century before Cockburn Street itself was carved through the Old Town in the 1850s to link up with Waverley Station. Behind the bar, a wooden gantry in ornate Robert Adam-style baroque, lined with mirrors, backs a serious whisky collection: more than fifty single malts, alongside real ales and the kind of framed old photographs of Edinburgh that turn up in every pub on this stretch of street. Sitting right on the border between the Old and New Towns, a few paces from the station, it's been catching travellers passing between the two halves of the city for longer than the street itself has existed.

name: The Piper's Rest
description: Tucked just behind the Tron, in the same planned square as several other pubs carved out of the 1780s South Bridge development, the Piper's Rest leans hard into a kind of Scottishness other Hunter Square bars only gesture at: dark wood, low light, malt whisky and gin lined up behind the bar, and live traditional music seven nights a week mixing old tunes with newer covers. It's a reminder that Hunter Square itself, despite feeling like an ancient huddle of Old Town buildings, is a relatively late arrival on the Royal Mile's timeline, laid out after 1786 once the controversial South Bridge scheme had finished clearing away the wynds that stood here before.

name: Royal Mile
description: You won't find 'Royal Mile' on a single street sign - it's a Victorian nickname, coined in the late 19th century, for a chain of streets that has no official name of its own. Walking downhill from the Castle to Holyroodhouse, the same road changes its name four times: Castlehill, then Lawnmarket, then High Street - the stretch you're on now - then Canongate. The name comes from the royal processional route once ridden between the two, and the distance really does work out to almost exactly one mile.
